questions.q: According to this lesson, why do an experienced reviewer's questions feel less unpredictable once you understand how review boards actually operate?
options: Because review boards are given a fixed script of questions they must ask in order
Because questions cluster into a small number of recurring categories that probe the same handful of failure classes in every design
Because most review boards only ask about cost and nothing else
Because questions are randomly generated and cannot actually be anticipated
questions.explain: Reviewer questions recur across designs because their job is to probe the same recurring failure classes — failure modes, cost at scale, blast radius, and complexity — not because any one design is uniquely scrutinized.

questions.q: The question "what happens when X fails" connects most directly to which earlier chapter's material?
options: Chapter 4, Resilience and Disaster Recovery
Chapter 5, Governance at Scale
Chapter 6, Architecture Decision Records
Chapter 1, Enterprise Cloud Architecture Principles only
questions.explain: The failure-mode question is the resilience question from Chapter 4, applied to the specific design under review — what happens to the component most likely to fail.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a review board asks "what does this cost at 10x scale" instead of just asking about current cost?
options: Because current cost is never relevant to a review board
Because designs that look fine at pilot scale can hide a cost curve that bends badly at higher volume, such as a tier boundary or egress charge
Because 10x is a fixed legal requirement for all cloud architecture reviews
Because cost questions are only asked when the design uses AWS, never Azure
questions.explain: A design's unit economics can look fine at small scale while hiding a cost cliff — a tiering boundary, egress charge, or per-seat licensing cost — that only shows up once volume grows.

questions.q: What does "security blast radius" refer to in a review-board question, as described in this lesson?
options: The physical size of the data center housing the workload
The number of engineers who have access to the production environment
What else is reachable or affected if one component is compromised, governed by the account and network boundaries covered in earlier chapters
The total dollar cost of a security incident
questions.explain: Blast radius asks what else becomes reachable if a given component is compromised — a question directly tied to the account-boundary and network-segmentation material from Chapters 2 and 3.

questions.q: How does this lesson say you should respond to "what's the simplest version of this"?
options: Treat it as an attack on the design and defend its complexity without further explanation
Refuse to answer, since simplicity isn't a legitimate review criterion
Explain specifically what the simpler version would give up, and why that tradeoff wasn't the one you made
Agree immediately to rebuild the design as the simplest possible version
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as a sincere operational question about ongoing complexity cost, best answered by describing the simpler alternative concretely and explaining why its tradeoff was rejected.
